newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary fin.min urges wage and price restraint.
newsitem.headline: Hungary fin.min urges wage and price restraint.

text.p: Hungarian Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy on Wednesday joined central bank head Gyorgy Suranyi in urging the government and social groups to agree to a programme of slashing inflation and curbing wage growth in 1998.

"It is realistic to expect that by this programme, (year-on-year) inflation will go down to nine percent by the end of 1998," he said, outlining his ideas about the measures needed for a drastic inflation cut to a conference of businessmen and journalists.

Hungary has been urged by the International Monetary Fund to adopt more ambitious plans for the reduction of average inflation than the originally targeted five percentage point cut both for 1997 and 1998, from 23.6 percent in 1996.
The Finance Ministry is preparing the 1998 budget draft in two versions, one of which would aim at a more radical reduction in inflation.

After Prime Minister Gyula Horn last week played down the importance of wage rises in generating inflation, National Bank of Hungary president Gyorgy Suranyi apparently contradicted Horn by saying the country would need a wide framework of price and wage agreements to cut inflation drastically.

Now, Medgyessy said a government agreement with trade unions and pensioners on 1998 wages and pension hikes would be one of the main conditions to getting year-on-year inflation down to single digit by the end of 1998.
He added that the government should also agree with the central bank on a schedule for the reduction of the rate of the forint's crawling peg devaluation, which is currently 1.2 percent monthly.
"By this, (the government) would also indicate that it believes its own words that inflation will be brought down," he said.

The framework of wage and price agreements should also include consensus with foreign investors in the energy sector about the mechanism of energy price adjustments and an accord with municipalities about local public service fees, the minister said.
The government must publish clear and detailed inflation forecasts for the next two years as in Hungary high inflation expectations hinder the cutting of the pace of price rises, Medgyessy said.
"The government will have to have a very clear-cut inflation prognosis, with almost monthly precision, " he said.
Medgyessy added that the government should also agree with its partners on possible measures it can use if prices or wages rise more quickly than planned.
He added that certain elements of the anti-inflationary measures planned for 1998 should already be applied in the second half of this year but did not elaborate.
Analysts said earlier that, with elections due in 1998, the government would find it difficult to reach a moderate wages and prices agreements even without real wage cuts.

Hungarian real wages have seen a slump of over 15 percent in the past two years and the government is currently facing the toughest challenge so far to its tax policies from farmers staging a three-day nation-wide blockade.

The Finance Ministry is engaged in talks with leaders of thousands of agricultural producers who have used farm vehicles to block many main roads since Monday in protest over 1997 tax and social security payments.
"This is a great programme," Medgyessy said about the anti-inflationary plans. "If we didn't have to be so busy putting out fires, it could even be wonderful."
